algorithms.name: Backtracking
algorithms.summary: Assign variables one at a time in a fixed order, trying values in order. If a value conflicts with an earlier assignment try the next; if none is left, go back to the previous variable (chronological backtracking).

algorithms.name: Forward checking
algorithms.summary: Combine search and reasoning: after assigning a variable, delete the values of its future neighbours that conflict with it. If some future domain becomes empty, backtrack at once instead of discovering the failure later.

algorithms.name: Arc consistency (AC-1, AC-3)
algorithms.summary: Delete every value that has no supporting value in a neighbouring variable. Revise(X, Y) removes unsupported values of X with respect to Y. AC-1 sweeps all arcs until nothing changes; AC-3 keeps a queue and re-examines only the arcs into a variable whose domain shrank.

algorithms.name: Waltz algorithm
algorithms.summary: Interpret a line drawing of a polyhedral scene. Each junction starts with every labelling its type allows (L, fork, arrow, T); a labelling survives only if each of its lines can get the same label from the junction at the other end. Propagate with an AC-3 style queue.

algorithms.name: Model-based diagnosis
algorithms.summary: Assume components work as their models say and propagate values through the circuit. A contradiction with an observation implicates the components whose models were used: a conflict set. A diagnosis is a minimal set of components that hits every conflict.

algorithms.name: Minimax
algorithms.summary: Evaluate the game tree depth-first from left to right: a MAX node takes the largest child value, a MIN node the smallest. The root's value is the outcome with best play from both sides.

algorithms.name: Alpha-Beta pruning
algorithms.summary: Carry a window (α, β): α is the best value MAX can already guarantee, β the best MIN can guarantee. When α ≥ β at a node, the remaining children cannot matter and are pruned.

algorithms.name: SSS*
algorithms.summary: A best-first algorithm for game trees. OPEN holds triples (node, LIVE or SOLVED, merit h). It refines the most promising strategy first and never evaluates a leaf that Alpha-Beta would prune; it can skip leaves Alpha-Beta evaluates.

algorithms.name: Best First Search
algorithms.summary: OPEN is a priority queue on h(N), the heuristic estimate of distance to the goal. Fast when h is good, not optimal.

algorithms.name: Hill Climbing
algorithms.summary: Move to the best-looking neighbour (lowest h) as long as it improves on the current node. Constant memory, but it stops at the first local optimum, which need not be the goal.

algorithms.name: Beam Search
algorithms.summary: Generate the children of every node in the beam and keep only the w best by h. Memory is bounded by w; a narrow beam can discard the only way to the goal.

algorithms.name: Uniform Cost Search
algorithms.summary: OPEN is a priority queue on g(N), the cost so far. A cheaper path to a node on OPEN or CLOSED updates its parent. Optimal for non-negative costs.

algorithms.name: A*
algorithms.summary: OPEN is a priority queue on f(N) = g(N) + w·h(N). With w = 1 and an admissible h (h ≤ h*) the first goal picked is optimal. w > 1 is weighted A*: faster, not guaranteed optimal.

algorithms.name: Admissibility & monotone check
algorithms.summary: Compute the true remaining cost h* by a backward Dijkstra from the goal, then test every node for admissibility (h ≤ h*) and every edge for the monotone condition h(m) ≤ k(m,n) + h(n).

algorithms.name: IDA*
algorithms.summary: Depth-first search that never expands a node with f = g + h above a bound. Start with bound f(S); after a failed pass, raise the bound to the smallest f that was cut off. Optimal with admissible h, memory linear in depth.

algorithms.name: Recursive Best-First Search
algorithms.summary: Explore the best child while its f stays below the best alternative elsewhere; when it exceeds that limit, back up its f value and switch. Keeps only the current path and its siblings.

algorithms.name: Divide & Conquer Frontier Search
algorithms.summary: Frontier search drops CLOSED: each OPEN node remembers which neighbours already used an edge to it, so expanded nodes are never regenerated. A relay node halfway along each path lets the path be rebuilt by two smaller searches.

algorithms.name: Breadth First Search
algorithms.summary: OPEN is a queue: new children are appended, so the shallowest node is expanded first. Finds a path with the fewest edges.

algorithms.name: Depth First Search
algorithms.summary: OPEN is a stack: new children are prepended, so the deepest node is expanded first. Little memory, no optimality.

algorithms.name: Depth First Iterative Deepening
algorithms.summary: Run depth-bounded DFS with bound 0, 1, 2, … until the goal is found. The path of BFS with the memory of DFS, at the price of repeated work.

algorithms.name: Forward state-space planning
algorithms.summary: Search forward from the initial state: every applicable operator gives a successor state. Breadth-first search returns a shortest plan, but the branching factor is the number of applicable actions.

algorithms.name: Backward state-space planning
algorithms.summary: Search backwards from the goal. An operator is relevant if it adds a goal and deletes none; regressing the goal set G through it gives (G − add) ∪ pre. Stop when the initial state satisfies the current goal set.

algorithms.name: Goal Stack Planning
algorithms.summary: Keep a stack of goals and actions. Pop satisfied goals; replace an unsatisfied goal by an action that achieves it plus that action's preconditions; when an action reaches the top its preconditions hold, so apply it. Goals are solved one at a time, which is why the Sussman anomaly makes it undo its own work.

algorithms.name: Partial Order Planning
algorithms.summary: Search in the space of partial plans. Start with steps Start (effects = initial state) and Finish (preconditions = goal). Repeatedly pick an open precondition, support it with an existing or a new step via a causal link, and resolve threats by promotion or demotion. Backtrack when stuck.

algorithms.name: AO*
algorithms.summary: Follow the marked (currently best) connectors from the start to an unexpanded node, expand it, then revise costs upwards: each node's cost is its cheapest connector, an AND connector costs the sum over its children. A node is solved when all children of its marked connector are solved.

algorithms.name: Forward chaining
algorithms.summary: Repeat the recognise–act cycle: match every rule against working memory to build the conflict set, choose one instantiation by a conflict-resolution strategy, fire it (add or remove facts), until no new instantiation remains.

algorithms.name: Rete algorithm
algorithms.summary: Compile the conditions into a network. Alpha nodes test one pattern and remember the facts that pass; beta (join) nodes combine partial matches with consistent variable bindings; terminal nodes feed the conflict set. A new fact only travels the paths it affects, so nothing is re-matched.

algorithms.name: Sequence alignment (dynamic programming)
algorithms.summary: Fill a table D(i,j) = cheapest alignment of the first i letters of a with the first j letters of b, one row at a time, then trace back the optimal path through the lattice.

algorithms.name: Sequence alignment (A*)
algorithms.summary: Treat each lattice point (i,j) as a state and search from (0,0) to (m,n) with A*. h(i,j) = gap × |(m−i) − (n−j)| never overestimates, because that many gaps are unavoidable.

algorithms.name: Nearest Neighbour
algorithms.summary: Grow one path from a start city, always moving to the closest unvisited city; return home at the end.

algorithms.name: Greedy heuristic
algorithms.summary: Scan edges shortest first; accept an edge unless a city would get degree 3 or a cycle shorter than n would close.

algorithms.name: Savings heuristic
algorithms.summary: Start with an out-and-back trip from the base to every city, then merge trips in decreasing order of savings S(i,j) = C(base,i) + C(base,j) − C(i,j).

algorithms.name: Brute force (exact)
algorithms.summary: Fix the first city and try every ordering of the rest; for a symmetric TSP each tour appears twice, so (n−1)!/2 distinct tours.

algorithms.name: Genetic algorithm
algorithms.summary: Population of tours. Roulette-wheel selection (fitness = K / cost), pairwise crossover, swap mutation, then the weakest members are replaced by the strongest offspring.

algorithms.name: Crossover lab
algorithms.summary: Apply one TSP crossover to two parents: cycle, PMX, order (path representation), alternating edges and heuristic (adjacency), ordinal + single-point, or naive single-point to see why it fails.

algorithms.name: Variable neighbourhood descent
algorithms.summary: Hill climb with a sparse neighbourhood, then continue from its local optimum with denser ones. A local optimum of one MoveGen need not be one of the next.

algorithms.name: Beam search
algorithms.summary: Keep the w best neighbours of all beam members at every level; stop when the best of the level is no better than the best so far. w = 1 is hill climbing.

algorithms.name: Tabu search
algorithms.summary: Always move to the best neighbour that is not tabu, even if it is worse. A move's key (the swapped pair / removed edges) stays tabu for tt iterations; aspiration allows a tabu move that beats bestSeen.

algorithms.name: Iterated hill climbing
algorithms.summary: Repeat: random start tour, steepest-descent hill climbing to a local optimum. Return the best local optimum found.

algorithms.name: Random walk
algorithms.summary: Pure exploration: ignore the evaluation function and step to a random neighbour each time, remembering the best tour seen.

algorithms.name: Simulated annealing
algorithms.summary: Pick a random neighbour and move to it with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), ΔE = cost(current) − cost(next). T falls geometrically: high T ≈ coin flip, T → 0 ≈ hill climbing.

algorithms.name: 2-city exchange
algorithms.summary: Swap the positions of any two cities: n(n−1)/2 neighbours. Steepest-descent hill climbing until no swap helps.

algorithms.name: 2-edge exchange (2-opt)
algorithms.summary: Remove two non-adjacent edges and reconnect the other way, which reverses the block between them: n(n−3)/2 neighbours.

algorithms.name: Or-opt (move a city)
algorithms.summary: Take one city out and insert it between two other neighbours: a special 3-edge exchange.

algorithms.name: 3-edge exchange
algorithms.summary: Remove three edges and reconnect the three segments in a new way (pure 3-opt moves).

algorithms.name: Ant colony optimisation
algorithms.summary: Each ant builds a tour city by city with P(i→j) ∝ τ^α (1/d)^β over unvisited cities. Then pheromone evaporates, τ ← (1−ρ)τ, and every ant deposits Q/L on the edges of its tour.
